title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 10 Oct 2026]
Title:FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at this https URL.

report.summary: New FDE-Bench benchmark shows AI agents struggle with end-to-end delivery from vague business requests, scoring far below human forward-deployed engineers.
report.background: Real-world business requests often omit key requirements because frontline practitioners rely on tacit, experience-based rules they cannot easily articulate. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) bridge this gap by eliciting missing requirements through dialogue and iteratively refining solutions until customers accept them. Existing optimization benchmarks usually start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often inject artificial information gaps into existing tasks. FDE-Bench is presented as the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery requiring interactive clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning, with clarification targets distilled from practitioner-FDE discussions. Agents must query a simulated customer, and evaluators compare final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, performance remains far below FDE level.
key_points: FDE-Bench contains 49 real customer cases across combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Unlike synthetic benchmarks, its missing requirements come from actual practitioner-FDE discussions, so agents must uncover tacit business rules through dialogue with a simulated customer rather than solving a fully specified problem.

The benchmark evaluates end-to-end delivery, not just final accuracy. Agents must clarify underspecified requests, iteratively optimize solutions, and produce artifacts judged against customer acceptance criteria, with customer-accepted FDE solutions serving as quality references. This tests the full workflow from ambiguous request to delivered solution.

Results across 18 agent configurations are weak. The highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510 against an FDE reference of 1.0, and the highest delivery success rate is just 6.12%, meaning agents rarely reach FDE-quality delivery on these underspecified real-world business tasks.

The findings suggest the main bottleneck is not coding or optimization alone, but requirement elicitation and iterative refinement under ambiguity. Benchmarks with explicit objectives or injected information gaps do not capture this interactive, customer-facing delivery challenge that FDEs handle routinely.
report.impact: The benchmark shifts attention from raw model capability to agentic delivery: asking the right questions, handling incomplete specifications, and iterating with feedback until acceptance. For the AI industry, it signals that reliable autonomous business delivery remains far from solved and that evaluation must include customer simulation and acceptance criteria, not just task accuracy. For developers, it highlights the need for agents that manage ambiguity, track evolving requirements, and integrate human or simulated feedback loops. For regular users, it means AI agents may still require significant human oversight for complex business automation. Expectations should be tempered: today’s agents can assist with well-scoped tasks, but FDE-level end-to-end delivery is not yet dependable.
report.tools: Follow the FDE-Bench project page and arXiv HTML for released data, evaluators, and code. Related open-source or accessible evaluation tools include Inspect AI for agentic evals, OpenAI Evals and promptfoo for structured testing, LangSmith or LangFuse for tracing iterative agent dialogue, and benchmarks such as τ-bench for user-agent interaction, SWE-bench for software delivery, and AgentBench or MLAgentBench for broader autonomous task evaluation.
